name: Daria Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm in at Bellwood Preserves by half eight. We make jams, chutneys and marmalade, a family firm of about 140 people, mostly on the factory floor. I'm one of three in marketing, so my day is product page copy, the weekly email, social posts, and planning next season's campaign with Margaret, who runs the team. Right now it's Christmas hampers, so it's a lot of 'give your gran something real' lines.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the product is real. I can walk downstairs and taste the damson batch before I write about it. What wears me out is the supermarket buyers, who want new pack copy every quarter and change their minds three times. I use AI tools every day for first drafts and for testing ten subject lines at once, which saves me about an hour a day, and I'm the one who taught the other two how.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Sami. He's an electrician and works with his uncle out of one van. We're getting married next September at my parents' church, where I still sing in the choir most Sundays. We've got about four months of bills saved, plus a separate wedding pot we don't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one isn't hard to picture, because some days it already feels like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd probably say I told you so, a little, because Tom, our designer, has been nervous for a year. Online I'd say the tools are useful helpers, not a replacement for knowing your customer. Nobody buys jam because a chatbot wrote a nice sentence; they buy it because it tastes like their nan's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I've built my little edge at Bellwood on being the person who's quickest with the tools, so if they stall, that edge stays small. But my job is safe, the firm's been steady for forty years, and that's worth a lot when you're paying for a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. I'd keep using the tools for drafts and subject lines, and push Margaret, who runs our team, to let me run a proper test of AI-written product pages on the online shop in spring. And I'd keep putting 300 a month into the wedding pot, because the venue deposit is due in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, like a storm that never came. But flat is fine when you're planning a wedding and, after that, a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a house. Where does that fit in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami and I want to buy in about three years, near my parents, so we're close when they get older. In this world that plan just stays on track: his van work, my salary, and we save for a deposit after the wedding. My dad keeps saying a family needs a front door of its own, and I agree with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Bellwood that worries you, even with AI stalling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket buyers, more than any robot. One big chain dropped our marmalade last year and a whole line on the factory floor went quiet for months. If another buyer walked away, the marketing budget would be the first thing the owners cut, so I keep an eye on that.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful helpers**, not a replacement for knowing your customer.
I'd tease Tom a little that his **year of worry** was for nothing.
think: I'd feel **relieved** my job is safe, and a bit disappointed my tool skills stay a small edge.
A steady **forty-year firm** matters a lot while we're paying for a wedding.
do: **Keep using** AI for first drafts and email subject lines, as I do now.
**Ask Margaret** to let me test AI-written product pages on the online shop in spring.
**Save 300 a month** into the wedding pot before the March deposit.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little flat, like a storm that never came.
S0.quote: Nobody buys jam because a chatbot wrote a nice sentence; they buy it because it tastes like their nan's.
fieldNote: Her real worry here is **supermarket buyers**, not AI; one lost contract already idled a factory line.
She treats her AI skill as a **personal edge** and is slightly let down when it stays small.
Family and **owning a home** near her parents shape every money decision she mentions.

steps.text: Keep writing Bellwood's weekly email and Christmas hamper copy as normal
Test AI-written product pages on Bellwood's online shop in spring
Put 300 a month into the wedding pot before March

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can see happening at Bellwood, honestly, and fairly soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the moment to get ahead of it, not hide from it. I'd offer to run a lunchtime session for the office staff, the buying team and customer service too, on how to use the tools well. Online I'd say what I always say: firms that adapt keep their people, and firms that don't go under and take everyone with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our team of three becomes two within a year or two. I think the cut lands on design, because the image tools are getting good at pack mock-ups, and I feel rotten saying that about Tom, who's a friend. I'm fairly confident I stay, because Margaret has already asked me to write the team's AI plan, and that's my job now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd make myself the person who owns all the AI work in marketing: write it down, set up the templates for product pages and the weekly email, so it's clearly mine. I'd do a three-month online course in marketing analytics in the evenings, so I can read the numbers and not just write the words. And I'd push our savings from four months towards six, even if the house slips a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way, not a frozen way. I'd rather be the one doing the changing at work than the one the changing is done to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel rotten about Tom. What would you actually say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the image tools now, this month, not when Margaret asks. He's brilliant with a pencil, but the brand needs someone who can turn twenty quick mock-ups into one good one. I'd sit with him on Friday afternoons and show him, because that's what I'd want someone to do for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change the wedding or the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the wedding; my mum would never forgive me, and the church is booked. The house probably slips six months while we build the bigger cushion. Sami's work is all hands-on, rewiring kitchens and fitting fuse boards, so his side looks solid, and that's a comfort.

say: I'd say this is the time to **get ahead** of AI, not hide from it.
I'd offer a **lunchtime session** on the tools for all the office staff.
I'd say firms that **adapt** keep their people, and firms that don't take everyone down.
think: Our **team of three** probably becomes two within a year or two.
The cut likely lands on **design**, and I feel rotten about my friend Tom.
I'm **fairly confident** I stay, because I'm already writing the team's AI plan.
do: **Take ownership** of all marketing AI work, with written templates for pages and emails.
**Study analytics** online for three months in the evenings.
**Grow savings** from four months towards six, letting the house slip.
feel: Glad to be **doing the changing**, not having it done to me.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one doing the changing at work than the one the changing is done to.
fieldNote: She expects a friend to lose his job and feels **guilty**, but plans to coach him on Fridays.
Her **confidence** rests on already owning the AI work, not on luck.
Her fiancé's **hands-on trade** is a quiet safety net she keeps coming back to.

steps.text: Set up AI templates for Bellwood's product pages and weekly email
Take a three-month evening course in marketing analytics
Build savings from four to six months, delaying the house six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's barely past our first wedding anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd stay steady. I'd say we've survived big changes before, and that people still want to buy from people they trust. At church I'd probably say what my dad says, that work is how we serve each other, and that isn't going away even if desks are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone. Everything I do is screen work: copy, emails, plans, the numbers. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, Bellwood doesn't need a marketing team; it needs Margaret and a subscription. Being good with the tools buys me maybe a year at the front of the queue, no more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrical apprenticeship as soon as I could get a place, probably with Sami's uncle, because hands-on work gets about three more years before the robots. Meanwhile I'd stay at Bellwood as long as they keep me and save every spare penny. And I'd shrink the wedding to a register office and lunch in the church hall, and put the venue money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest, more than I'd show anyone. But there's a plan, and having a plan is what stops me lying awake all night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd shrink the wedding. How would that conversation with your mum go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. My mum's been planning that day since I was about nine. I'd tell my mum that a big wedding is one day, and a paid-off van and a trade are the next forty years. I think she'd come round, because that's how she and my dad started too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trade buys about three more years. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't answer. Three years after AGI, robots come for rewiring too, so Sami and I would both be exposed by about 2031. I'd hope people still want someone they know in their home, fixing their fuse box, and that a small family firm with a good name counts for something. But I don't know, and I won't pretend I do.

say: I'd say people still want to **buy from people** they trust.
At church I'd repeat my dad's line that **work is service**, even if desks go.
think: My **marketing job** is gone, because all of it is screen work.
Bellwood would need Margaret and **a subscription**, not a team of three.
Being good with AI buys me **about a year**, no more.
do: **Start an electrical apprenticeship** with Sami's uncle as soon as a place opens.
**Save every spare penny** while Bellwood still pays me.
**Shrink the wedding** to a register office and a church hall lunch.
feel: Having **a plan** is what keeps me from lying awake.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum that a big wedding is one day, and a paid-off van and a trade are the next forty years.
fieldNote: She reads her own job as fully **exposed** and doesn't hide behind her AI skill.
Her move to a **trade** fits her belief in apprenticeships over handouts.
She admits the trade only buys **three years** before robots reach rewiring too.
Cutting the wedding is the **hardest trade-off**, mostly because of her mother.

steps.text: Apply for an electrical apprenticeship place within six months
Move from Bellwood marketing into Sami's uncle's electrical firm
Save every spare penny, including the wedding venue money
Swap the big wedding for a register office and church hall lunch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a different feeling. Still fast, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a smart firm to get ready, and I'd want Bellwood to be one of those. I'd post something about young people taking trades seriously again, because I've thought that for ages anyway. I'd stay away from the doom posts; they don't help anyone pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd squeeze everything I could out of marketing for the first three years. With AI doing more each year, the person who runs it becomes very valuable for a while, and I'd want a pay rise out of that. But I'd know the clock's running, and I'd start my way out by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at Bellwood and ask for a senior title and more pay by next summer, since I'd be running the AI side of marketing. Start doing the marketing for Sami's electrical business on weekends now: a proper website, local reviews, a booking page, so it grows into something we both work in. Then in year three, start an evening electrical course so I can do hands-on jobs too, before the robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a working kind of anxious. Five years feels like enough time to build a family business with my fiancé Sami, as long as we don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Sami's business rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's ours, and because people let a local electrician into their house on trust. My grandad ran a corner shop for thirty years on that kind of trust. If I can help the firm grow from one van to three, that's real jobs for people in our town, not just for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hold back from, in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, probably. I wouldn't want a big mortgage when both our incomes could change by 2034. We'd rent a bit longer and put the deposit into a second van and tools instead, which my dad would hate, but it's the safer bet.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for a smart firm to get ready.
I'd post about young people taking **trades seriously** again.
I'd **avoid doom posts**, because they don't help anyone pay a mortgage.
think: Whoever runs AI in marketing becomes **very valuable** for a while.
I'd want **a pay rise** out of those first three years.
I'd start **my way out** of marketing by year three.
do: **Ask for** a senior title and more pay by next summer.
**Build Sami's** website, reviews and booking page on weekends.
**Start an evening** electrical course in year three, before robots arrive around 2034.
feel: Five years feels like **enough time**, if we don't waste it.
S3.quote: Five years feels like enough time to build a family business with my fiancé Sami, as long as we don't waste it.
fieldNote: She sees a short **window of value** in running AI, and wants to cash it in.
The **family business** is her real plan; marketing becomes a bridge.
She would delay **buying a house**, against her father's wishes, to fund a second van.

steps.text: Stay at Bellwood and ask for a senior title by next summer
Build a website, reviews and booking page for Sami's electrical firm
Start an evening electrical course in the third year
Put the house deposit into a second van and tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole chunk of life before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, if people use it. I'd tell friends to stop arguing about whether it's coming and pick what they want to be doing in 2036. And I'd still say it online: learn a trade, learn the tools, and don't wait for the government to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for most of that decade, and that's sort of dangerous, because it'd be easy to coast. I could get to head of marketing somewhere by 33, earn well, and then lose it all in 2036. I'd have to be strict with myself to plan for the end while the middle feels good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing in marketing and keep using the tools every day, because the next five years would pay well. We'd buy the house after the wedding, with a mortgage we could pay on Sami's income alone, so we're safe when my side goes. And around 2031 I'd start moving into Sami's business properly, with bookings, quotes and some lighter hands-on work, and the training to match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Uneasy still, but mostly about whether I'd stay disciplined, not about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You might be thinking about children by then. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. We'd want two children, and I'd want to be home with them while they're small, the way my mum was with us. Knowing my marketing job ends around 2036 almost makes that easier, because I'd step back anyway and come back into Sami's firm, not into an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be helping people through that decade, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms and families first. Bellwood could fund apprenticeships for its own office staff, and churches could connect young people with tradespeople who need extra hands. I'd rather have that than a monthly payment. A cheque from the government doesn't give you a reason to get up in the morning.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, if people actually use it.
I'd tell friends to **learn a trade** and the tools, not wait for government.
think: Most of the decade would **pay well**, which makes coasting tempting.
I could reach **head of marketing** by 33 and still lose it in 2036.
do: **Buy the house** after the wedding, with a mortgage Sami's income covers alone.
**Keep climbing** in marketing and using AI tools every day.
**Move into** Sami's firm around 2031, with training for lighter hands-on work.
feel: **Calmer**, with the worry now about my own **discipline**, not money.
S4.quote: A cheque from the government doesn't give you a reason to get up in the morning.
fieldNote: With time, she makes **Sami's income** the anchor for the mortgage.
She plans to step back for **children**, then return to the family firm, not an office.
Her idea of help is **firms and families**, not government payments.

steps.text: Keep working towards head of marketing over the next five years
Use AI tools daily to stay the go-to person at Bellwood
Buy a house after the wedding on a mortgage Sami's pay covers
Plan two children and a move into Sami's firm around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't long enough to finish an apprenticeship, and it would hit Sami and me within the same few years. What would help is fast, paid apprenticeships for people like me leaving desk work, run by real firms, and help with rent while we train, as a loan we pay back, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd say to the younger ones in my family. My cousin Leila is sixteen and wants to do marketing like me. I'd tell my cousin Leila to learn a trade first, because a good pair of hands will be worth more than a good sentence.

headlineQuote: I'd tell my cousin Leila to learn a trade first, because a good pair of hands will be worth more than a good sentence.
portrait: Daria, 27, writes copy and plans campaigns at **Bellwood Preserves**, a family jam maker.
She is her team's **AI enthusiast**, using the tools daily and teaching colleagues.
Her life centres on her **fiancé Sami**, an electrician, their wedding and her church.
The faster AGI comes, the sooner she plans to switch into an **electrical trade** beside Sami.
She favours **apprenticeships** and family firms over government payments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to finish an apprenticeship.
It would hit her and Sami's **two incomes** within the same few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast, paid apprenticeships** run by real firms for people leaving desk work.
A **rent loan** while training, paid back, not a handout.
